docs.title: 🔗 LangChain AI Project
docs.text:
A production-ready, full-stack AI agent platform — multi-provider LLMs, agentic RAG, human-in-the-loop approvals, 14 tools, context management, and a streaming React UI.

Get Started View on GitHub

docs.title: What is this project?
docs.text: This is a fully working, deeply documented reference implementation for building production AI applications with the LangChain ecosystem. It is not a toy — it is a boilerplate you clone, configure with your API keys, and run. Every file is written to be readable, so you can understand the pattern and adapt it to your own product.

docs.title: Feature highlights
docs.text:
• Three LangGraph Agents

    A tool-using Assistant, an agentic Documents agent that retrieves, grades, rewrites and cites, and a Researcher that plans, gets your approval, researches steps in parallel, then writes a report.

    The three agents

  • Human-in-the-Loop

    The graph pauses with interrupt() before sending emails, running code, writing files, or starting research. You approve, edit the arguments, or reject with feedback — and the pause survives a page reload.

    How HITL works

  • 8 LLM Providers

    OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, xAI Grok, OpenRouter, Groq and Ollama behind one factory. Switch provider and model per conversation from the UI — no restart needed.

    Provider guide

  • Agentic RAG

    Upload PDF, Markdown, CSV or JSON. Chunks are embedded (OpenAI, Google, Ollama or local HuggingFace), stored in Chroma, retrieved with MMR, graded for relevance, and cited in the answer.

    RAG deep dive

  • LCEL Playground

    Five runnable chains you can try in the UI: summarize, translate, structured extraction (Pydantic), parallel analysis (RunnableParallel), and routing (RunnableBranch). All in one file.

    LCEL chains

  • Context Management

    Older turns are automatically summarized into a rolling summary field and removed from the history. The last N messages stay verbatim. Token trimming acts as a safety net. All three agents share this.

    Context management

  • Streaming UI

    Tokens stream over Server-Sent Events. Every tool call and agent step appears live on a "trace rail" alongside the answer. The approval gate uses a saffron highlight so it is impossible to miss.

    Streaming internals

  • 14 Built-in Tools

    Web search, Wikipedia, URL fetch, weather, calculator, datetime, document search, save/search memory, list/read/write files, Python REPL, and simulated email — all discoverable in the UI.

    Tool catalog

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/javaidgithub/langchain-ai-project.git
cd langchain-ai-project
make setup          # create .env, install backend + frontend deps
# edit .env and add at least one provider key
make backend        # API on :8000
make frontend       # UI  on :5173

Or with Docker in one command:

cp .env.example .env   # add your keys
docker compose up --build
# open http://localhost:8080

Full setup guide

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This document explains the decisions behind the project. For setup and usage see the README.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
React UI  ──SSE/REST──▶  FastAPI  ──▶  LangGraph graph  ──▶  LangChain (models, tools, retrievers)
                                              │
                                    checkpointer (SQLite) + store (memory)
  • API layer (app/api): thin. Validates input, selects the graph, returns a StreamingResponse.
  • Streaming service (app/services/streaming.py): the only place that knows LangGraph's stream format. It converts it into the stable event protocol below, so the UI never depends on LangGraph internals.
  • Agents (app/agents): pure graph logic. They read per-request options from config["configurable"] through AgentConfig, so one compiled graph serves every provider, model and tool selection.
  • Tools / RAG / chains: plain LangChain code with no knowledge of HTTP.

docs.title: Why one compiled graph, many models
docs.text: Graphs are compiled once at startup with the shared checkpointer and store. The model is not baked in: each node calls get_chat_model(provider, model, temperature) using values from the run config. That is what makes provider switching a UI dropdown rather than a redeploy, and a conversation can even change model between turns.

docs.title: Per-request API keys
docs.text: Keys pasted in the UI travel in the request body and are stored in a ContextVar (core/context.py), not in config["configurable"]. LangGraph copies configurable values into checkpoint metadata, so putting a secret there could persist it. The context variable lives only for the request. resolve_api_key prefers the per-request key and falls back to the server environment.

docs.title: Stream events
docs.text:
POST /api/chat/stream and POST /api/chat/resume return text/event-stream. Each frame is data: <json>\n\n.

type Payload Meaning start thread_id Run started (new threads get their id here) step node A graph node finished token content, node Assistant text delta reasoning content Reasoning-model thinking delta tool_call id, name, args The model requested a tool tool_result tool_call_id, name, content, status Tool finished (status is success or error) context summary Older turns were compacted plan plan Research plan produced sources sources[] RAG citations usage token counts, llm_calls Aggregated by the callback handler interrupt id, value Run paused for a human decision error message Friendly error; the stream still ends with done done interrupted Always the last event

The generator never raises. Provider errors (bad key, rate limit, recursion limit) become error events with actionable text.

Only nodes listed in AGENTS[...]["stream_nodes"] stream tokens to the user. Internal LLM calls (grading, planning, summarizing) do not leak into the chat. If a streamed node produces a full message without tokens (a provider that does not stream, or a static message), the full text is emitted once.

docs.title: Human-in-the-loop protocol
docs.text:
1. A node calls interrupt(payload). LangGraph saves a checkpoint and stops the run.
  2. After the stream ends, the service reads graph.aget_state(...) and emits an interrupt event for each pending interrupt, then done with interrupted: true. Reading from state (rather than only from the stream) is more robust across LangGraph versions and also powers reload.
  3. The client posts {thread_id, decision, ...options} to /api/chat/resume. The service runs the graph with Command(resume=decision). The node re-executes from the start and interrupt() now returns decision.

Because the node re-runs, code before interrupt() must be idempotent. The approval nodes only read state before interrupting.

Edit works by replacing the AI message that holds the tool calls. A message with the same id replaces the original through the add_messages reducer.

Reject adds a ToolMessage (with status="error") for every tool call in that AI message and routes back to the agent. Every tool call must receive a result or providers reject the next request, which is why rejecting applies to all calls in the batch.

docs.title: Context management
docs.text:
See app/agents/context.py. The summarizer is a graph node that runs first on every turn, so all three agents get it. It only fires above the token budget, so short chats pay nothing.

Token counts use count_tokens_approximately, which is fast and provider-independent. For exact budgets, replace it with the provider's tokenizer.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text: Data Store Notes Conversation state, pending interrupts LangGraph checkpointer (data/checkpoints.db) Keyed by thread_id Sidebar index (title, agent, timestamps) data/app.db The checkpointer has no cheap "list threads" Vector store Chroma (data/chroma) One collection, chunks tagged with source Long-term memory LangGraph InMemoryStore Lost on restart; swap for Postgres Agent workspace and email outbox data/workspace Sandboxed file tools

docs.title: Scaling out
docs.text:
SQLite and the in-memory store assume one process. For several replicas:

# app/services/checkpointer.py
from langgraph.checkpoint.postgres.aio import AsyncPostgresSaver

@asynccontextmanager
async def create_checkpointer(settings):
    async with AsyncPostgresSaver.from_conn_string(settings.database_url) as saver:
        await saver.setup()   # creates tables on first run
        yield saver

Install langgraph-checkpoint-postgres and psycopg[binary,pool], and add a database_url setting. Use the matching Postgres store for long-term memory in main.py, and move ThreadRepository to the same database. Replace Chroma's local persistence with a client/server vector database. Long agent runs hold an HTTP connection open, so tune proxy and load balancer timeouts.

docs.title: Frontend design notes
docs.text:
• Trace rail. Tool calls, retrieval steps, plans and context compaction are rendered as nodes on a vertical rail beside the answer. A node is a spinner while running, a filled dot when done, and a saffron square while waiting on the human. The approval gate uses the same saffron so the pause is unmistakable.
  • State. Three small Zustand stores: settings (persisted), chat (ephemeral) and catalog (server metadata). hooks/chatActions.ts is the only code that mutates chat state from stream events.
  • Reload safety. Opening a thread rebuilds messages from server history and re-attaches any pending interrupt.
  • Accessibility. Visible focus, labelled controls, role="alertdialog" on the approval gate, reduced-motion support, light and dark themes via prefers-color-scheme.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Contributions are welcome. This is a reference project, so clarity and teaching value matter as much as functionality.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/javaidgithub/langchain-ai-project.git
cd langchain-ai-project
make setup

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text:
make test    # backend pytest + frontend typecheck
make lint    # ruff on backend

The backend tests run the real LangGraph graphs through the real HTTP and SSE layer using a scripted fake model — no API keys needed.

docs.title: Adding an agent
docs.text:
1. Build a StateGraph in backend/app/agents/.
  2. Register it in backend/app/agents/registry.py.
  3. Add the id to AgentName in backend/app/schemas/chat.py and AgentId in frontend/src/api/types.ts.

docs.title: Code style
docs.text:
• Backend: Python 3.11+, ruff for lint, type hints everywhere.
  • Frontend: TypeScript strict mode, no any except in explicit casts.
  • Docstrings on every tool — the model reads them.

docs.title: Opening an issue
docs.text:
Please include:

  • The provider and model you were using
  • The full error message from the browser or terminal
  • Relevant .env settings (redact API keys)

docs.title: POST /api/chat/stream
docs.text:
Send a message. Returns a text/event-stream response.

Body 

{
  "message": "What is the capital of France?",
  "thread_id": null,
  "agent": "assistant",
  "model": {
    "provider": "openai",
    "model": "gpt-4o-mini",
    "temperature": 0.2,
    "api_key": null
  },
  "enabled_tools": null,
  "require_approval": true,
  "system_prompt": null
}

  • thread_id — omit or null to start a new thread; provide an existing id to continue.
  • enabled_tools — null means all tools enabled; an empty list means no tools.
  • api_key — optional per-request key; stored in memory only.

See Stream Events for the response format.

docs.text:

docs.title: Request Schemas
docs.text: Key Pydantic models. All are validated by FastAPI before the handler runs.

docs.title: ModelSelection
docs.text:
class ModelSelection(BaseModel):
    provider: str          # e.g. "openai", "anthropic", "gemini"
    model: str             # e.g. "gpt-4o-mini" — any id your provider supports
    temperature: float     # 0.0–2.0, default 0.2
    api_key: str | None    # per-request key; never stored

docs.title: ChatRequest
docs.text:
class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
    message: str                   # 1–20000 characters
    thread_id: str | None          # null to start a new thread
    agent: "assistant" | "rag" | "research"
    model: ModelSelection
    enabled_tools: list[str] | None  # null = all tools; [] = no tools
    require_approval: bool           # default True
    system_prompt: str | None        # max 4000 characters

docs.title: ResumeRequest
docs.text:
class ResumeRequest(BaseModel):
    thread_id: str
    agent: "assistant" | "rag" | "research"
    model: ModelSelection
    decision: dict     # see Human-in-the-Loop docs for decision shapes

docs.title: ChainRequest
docs.text:
class ChainRequest(BaseModel):
    model: ModelSelection
    inputs: dict[str, str]   # keys depend on the chain (see GET /api/chains)

docs.title: Stream Events
docs.text:
POST /api/chat/stream and POST /api/chat/resume both return text/event-stream. Each frame is:

data: <json>\n\n

The stream always ends with a done event.

docs.title: start
docs.text:
The run has begun. New threads get their id here.

{ "type": "start", "thread_id": "abc123" }

docs.title: step
docs.text:
A graph node has finished. Used to power the trace rail.

{ "type": "step", "node": "manage_context" }

Possible nodes: manage_context, agent, tools, human_approval, prepare, retrieve, grade, rewrite, generate, planner, approve_plan, research_one, writer, cancel.

docs.title: token
docs.text:
An assistant text delta. Concatenate these to build the full reply.

{ "type": "token", "content": "Paris is", "node": "agent" }

docs.title: reasoning
docs.text:
A reasoning-model thinking delta (e.g. deepseek-reasoner). Shown in a collapsible block.

{ "type": "reasoning", "content": "Let me think..." }

docs.title: tool_call
docs.text:
The model has requested a tool. Appears before the tool runs.

{ "type": "tool_call", "id": "call_1", "name": "web_search", "args": { "query": "langchain 2025" } }

docs.title: tool_result
docs.text:
A tool has finished.

{
  "type": "tool_result",
  "tool_call_id": "call_1",
  "name": "web_search",
  "content": "LangChain released version...",
  "status": "success"
}

status is "success" or "error". A rejected tool has status: "error" and content starting with "The user rejected".

docs.title: context
docs.text:
Older messages were summarized. The summary is the updated rolling context.

{ "type": "context", "summary": "User asked about Paris. Agent confirmed it is the capital of France." }

docs.title: plan
docs.text:
The Researcher produced a research plan.

{ "type": "plan", "plan": ["History of Paris", "Paris economy", "Paris tourism"] }

docs.title: sources
docs.text:
RAG citations from the Documents agent.

{
  "type": "sources",
  "sources": [
    { "index": 1, "source": "report.pdf", "page": 3, "snippet": "Paris is the capital..." }
  ]
}

docs.title: usage
docs.text:
Aggregated token usage for the run.

{ "type": "usage", "input_tokens": 412, "output_tokens": 89, "total_tokens": 501, "llm_calls": 2 }

docs.title: interrupt
docs.text:
The run is paused for a human decision. The stream ends after this.

Tool approval: 

{
  "type": "interrupt",
  "id": "interrupt_id_1",
  "value": {
    "type": "tool_approval",
    "message": "The agent wants to run the following action(s). Approve, edit, or reject.",
    "tool_calls": [
      { "id": "call_1", "name": "send_email", "args": { "to": "a@b.com", "subject": "Hi", "body": "Hello" }, "needs_approval": true }
    ]
  }
}

Plan approval: 

{
  "type": "interrupt",
  "id": "interrupt_id_2",
  "value": {
    "type": "plan_approval",
    "message": "Review the research plan. Approve, edit the steps, or cancel.",
    "plan": ["Step 1", "Step 2"]
  }
}

docs.title: error
docs.text:
A friendly error message. The stream still ends with done.

{ "type": "error", "message": "No API key for OpenAI. Add it to your .env file or paste it in Settings." }

docs.title: done
docs.text:
Always the last event. interrupted: true means the run paused for human input.

{ "type": "done", "interrupted": false }

docs.title: Handling interrupts
docs.text:
When done.interrupted is true:

  1. Read the interrupt event(s) — there is one per pending approval.
  2. Show the approval UI.
  3. When the user decides, POST /api/chat/resume with { thread_id, agent, model, decision }.
  4. The stream resumes from the saved checkpoint.

If the user reloads the page before deciding, GET /api/threads/{thread_id} returns interrupts: [...] so you can re-show the approval UI.

docs.title: Callbacks & Observability
docs.text:
LangChain's callback system lets you hook into model calls, tool executions and chain events without modifying their code.

Source file: backend/app/callbacks/usage.py

docs.title: The UsageCallback
docs.text:
Every run attaches a UsageCallback that aggregates token counts and tool timings:

class UsageCallback(AsyncCallbackHandler):
    def __init__(self):
        self.input_tokens = 0
        self.output_tokens = 0
        self.llm_calls = 0

    async def on_llm_end(self, response, **kwargs):
        self.llm_calls += 1
        for generations in response.generations:
            for gen in generations:
                usage = getattr(gen.message, "usage_metadata", None)
                if usage:
                    self.input_tokens += usage.get("input_tokens", 0)
                    self.output_tokens += usage.get("output_tokens", 0)

    async def on_tool_start(self, serialized, input_str, *, run_id, **kwargs):
        self._tool_started[run_id] = time.perf_counter()

    async def on_tool_end(self, output, *, run_id, **kwargs):
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - self._tool_started.pop(run_id, 0)
        log.info("tool finished in %.0f ms", elapsed * 1000)

At the end of each run, the totals are emitted as a usage stream event and displayed under the assistant reply.

docs.title: Available callback hooks
docs.text: Method Fires when on_llm_start / on_llm_end A model call starts / finishes on_chat_model_stream A streaming chunk arrives on_tool_start / on_tool_end A tool starts / finishes on_chain_start / on_chain_end A chain (LCEL runnable) starts / finishes on_retriever_start / on_retriever_end A retriever runs on_llm_error / on_tool_error An error occurs

docs.title: LangSmith tracing
docs.text:
For full distributed tracing, enable LangSmith:

LANGSMITH_TRACING=true
LANGSMITH_API_KEY=ls__...
LANGSMITH_PROJECT=langchain-ai-project

LangSmith captures every run — inputs, outputs, tool calls, intermediate steps, latency and token counts — in a web dashboard. You can replay, compare and debug runs there.

Get a free API key at smith.langchain.com.

docs.title: LLM caching
docs.text:
Enable response caching to skip redundant model calls during development:

ENABLE_LLM_CACHE=true

# backend/app/main.py
from langchain_core.caches import InMemoryCache
from langchain_core.globals import set_llm_cache
set_llm_cache(InMemoryCache())

Identical (prompt, model) pairs return the cached result instantly. Useful when testing prompts. Not recommended in production — it can return stale responses.

docs.title: Structured logs
docs.text:
The app uses Python's standard logging. Set LOG_LEVEL in .env:

LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG   # DEBUG | INFO | WARNING | ERROR

Noisy libraries (httpx, httpcore, chromadb) are pinned to WARNING regardless of LOG_LEVEL.

docs.title: Context Management
docs.text:
LLMs have a finite context window. Long conversations would eventually overflow it — and sending thousands of tokens on every turn is expensive. This project uses a three-layer approach.

Source file: backend/app/agents/context.py

docs.title: Layer 1 — Summarize old turns
docs.text:
A manage_context node runs at the start of every agent turn. If the history exceeds MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS, it:

  1. Finds a safe split point (always on a HumanMessage, so a tool call is never separated from its result).
  2. Calls the model to summarize the old turns into the running summary field.
  3. Removes the old messages with RemoveMessage.
async def manage_context(state, config):
    if count_tokens_approximately(messages) <= MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS:
        return {}   # nothing to do
    old = messages[:split]
    new_summary = await llm.ainvoke(SUMMARY_PROMPT.format(
        summary=state.get("summary") or "(none yet)",
        transcript=get_buffer_string(old),
    ))
    return {
        "summary": new_summary,
        "messages": [RemoveMessage(id=m.id) for m in old],
    }

The summary field is part of AgentState and is persisted in the checkpointer, so it survives restarts.

docs.title: Layer 2 — Inject the summary
docs.text:
Before every model call, the summary is prepended to the system prompt:

def build_prompt_messages(system: str, state) -> list[AnyMessage]:
    if state.get("summary"):
        system += f"\n\nSummary of earlier conversation:\n{state['summary']}"
    history = trim_messages(state["messages"], ...)
    return [SystemMessage(content=system), *history]

The model always has access to the full conversation context — either as live messages or as the summary.

docs.title: Layer 3 — Trim as a safety net
docs.text:
trim_messages hard-limits what is actually sent:

from langchain_core.messages.utils import trim_messages, count_tokens_approximately

history = trim_messages(
    messages,
    max_tokens=MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS,
    strategy="last",                  # keep the most recent
    token_counter=count_tokens_approximately,
    start_on="human",                 # never start on a tool result
    include_system=False,
    allow_partial=False,
)

count_tokens_approximately is fast and provider-independent. For exact counts, swap in tiktoken or the provider's own tokenizer.

docs.title: Why split on a HumanMessage?
docs.text:
Tool call sequences look like:

HumanMessage  → AIMessage (with tool_calls) → ToolMessage (result) → AIMessage

If you cut in the middle (e.g., before the ToolMessage), the model receives an AIMessage with tool calls but no results. OpenAI and Anthropic both reject this. The split function walks backward from the target index until it finds a HumanMessage:

def find_split_index(messages, keep_last):
    idx = len(messages) - keep_last
    while idx > 0 and not isinstance(messages[idx], HumanMessage):
        idx -= 1
    return max(idx, 0)

docs.title: Long-term vs. short-term
docs.text:
Short-term Long-term What Conversation history Facts, preferences Where LangGraph checkpointer (SQLite) LangGraph InMemoryStore Scope One thread All threads for a user Survives restart Yes (SQLite) No (in-memory — use Postgres in production) How to use Automatic save_memory / search_memory tools

See Memory for long-term memory details.

docs.title: Human-in-the-Loop
docs.text:
Human-in-the-loop (HITL) means the agent pauses and waits for a human decision before proceeding. LangGraph implements this natively with interrupt().

Source files: backend/app/agents/assistant.py, backend/app/agents/research.py

docs.title: How interrupt() works
docs.text:
from langgraph.types import interrupt, Command

def human_approval(state: AgentState) -> Command:
    # 1. Pause the graph. Checkpoint is saved. Control returns to the caller.
    decision = interrupt({
        "type": "tool_approval",
        "tool_calls": [...]   # payload shown to the user
    })
    # 2. When resumed, interrupt() returns whatever the caller passed.
    if decision["action"] == "approve":
        return Command(goto="tools")
    elif decision["action"] == "edit":
        ...
    else:  # reject
        return Command(goto="agent", update={"messages": [rejection_message]})

The key insight: interrupt() saves state and stops the graph. When the caller later calls graph.ainvoke(Command(resume=decision), config), the graph reloads from the checkpoint and interrupt() returns decision as if it had never paused.

docs.title: Approve
docs.text:
{ "action": "approve" }
Runs the tool with its original arguments.

docs.title: Edit
docs.text:
{
  "action": "edit",
  "edited_args": {
    "call_id_1": { "to": "corrected@email.com", "subject": "...", "body": "..." }
  }
}
Replaces the AI message with one carrying updated tool call arguments, then runs the tools.

docs.title: Reject
docs.text:
{ "action": "reject", "feedback": "Don't email that address." }
Adds a ToolMessage with status="error" for every pending tool call, then routes back to the agent. The model sees the rejection message and can respond intelligently.

Important

Every tool call in a batch must receive a result. Sending an AI message with tool calls and then asking the model another question without tool results will cause a provider error. Rejection creates synthetic results so the history stays valid.

docs.title: Which tools require approval
docs.text:
Set in backend/app/tools/registry.py:

ToolSpec(send_email,   "communication", requires_approval=True),
ToolSpec(python_repl,  "code",          requires_approval=True),
ToolSpec(write_file,   "files",         requires_approval=True),

Any tool with requires_approval=True triggers the approval node. The routing function checks this:

def route_after_agent(state, config):
    calls = state["messages"][-1].tool_calls
    if AgentConfig.from_config(config).require_approval:
        if any(requires_approval(c["name"]) for c in calls):
            return "human_approval"
    return "tools"

docs.title: Survives page reloads
docs.text:
Because the graph state lives in the SQLite checkpointer, a pending approval survives:

  • Page reloads
  • Server restarts (with CHECKPOINTER=sqlite)
  • Network interruptions

GET /api/threads/{id} reads the checkpoint and returns any pending interrupts in the response. The frontend re-shows the approval gate when the thread is opened.

docs.title: Plan approval (Researcher)
docs.text:
The Researcher uses the same mechanism, but the payload is a plan instead of tool calls:

decision = interrupt({
    "type": "plan_approval",
    "plan": ["step 1", "step 2", "step 3"]
})

Decisions: approve, edit (with a plan array), or cancel.

docs.title: Disabling approval
docs.text: Set require_approval: false in the request body, or toggle Ask before risky actions off in the Settings panel. This is stored per session in the browser.

docs.title: LangChain Core
docs.text: langchain-core defines the base abstractions that everything else builds on. You rarely import it directly, but understanding it makes the rest click.

docs.title: The Runnable interface
docs.text:
Every LangChain component — a prompt, a model, an output parser, a retriever, a chain — implements Runnable. This means they all share the same interface:

component.invoke(input)           # synchronous, returns output
await component.ainvoke(input)    # async
component.stream(input)           # synchronous iterator of chunks
await component.astream(input)    # async iterator
component.batch([input1, input2]) # parallel batch

Because they share one interface, you can pipe them with |:

chain = prompt | model | parser
result = await chain.ainvoke({"text": "Hello"})

This is LCEL — the LangChain Expression Language. See LCEL Chains.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Chat models exchange BaseMessage objects, not raw strings:

from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage, AIMessage, SystemMessage, ToolMessage

messages = [
    SystemMessage(content="You are a helpful assistant."),
    HumanMessage(content="What is 2+2?"),
    AIMessage(content="4"),
]

AIMessage can carry tool_calls — structured requests for tools — and ToolMessage carries the results back. This is how tool use works in all three agents.

docs.title: Prompt templates
docs.text:
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", "You are a {role}. Answer in {language}."),
    ("human", "{question}"),
])
# Filled at runtime:
filled = prompt.invoke({"role": "chef", "language": "French", "question": "How do I make roux?"})

docs.title: Output parsers
docs.text:
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser
parser = StrOutputParser()
# Extracts the text content from an AIMessage
chain = prompt | model | parser

For structured data, use .with_structured_output(MyPydanticModel) — see LCEL Chains.

docs.title: Source files
docs.text: File What it shows backend/app/agents/prompts.py System prompts as string templates backend/app/chains/lcel.py Prompt templates, parsers and structured output backend/app/agents/context.py Message manipulation with RemoveMessage, trim_messages

docs.title: LangGraph Agents
docs.text:
LangGraph is LangChain's framework for building stateful, multi-step agent graphs. Where LCEL chains are linear pipelines, LangGraph graphs can loop, branch, pause for human input and fan out in parallel.

Source files: backend/app/agents/

docs.title: State
docs.text:
Every graph has a State TypedDict. Nodes read from it and return updates to it. LangGraph merges updates automatically using reducers.

from langgraph.graph import MessagesState

class AgentState(MessagesState):
    # MessagesState provides `messages: Annotated[list[AnyMessage], add_messages]`
    # add_messages reducer appends new messages rather than replacing the list
    summary: str   # our addition: a rolling summary of older turns

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
Nodes are async def functions that take the state and return a dict of updates:

async def agent_node(state: AgentState, config: RunnableConfig) -> dict:
    llm = get_chat_model(...)
    response = await llm.bind_tools(tools).ainvoke(messages, config)
    return {"messages": [response]}   # appended by the add_messages reducer

docs.title: Edges
docs.text:
Edges connect nodes. Conditional edges choose the next node at runtime:

graph.add_conditional_edges(
    "agent",
    route_after_agent,   # function that returns a node name or END
    {"tools": "tools", "human_approval": "human_approval", END: END},
)

docs.title: Compilation and persistence
docs.text:
graph = builder.compile(
    checkpointer=checkpointer,   # SQLite: conversations survive restarts
    store=store,                 # cross-thread long-term memory
)

docs.title: The Assistant graph
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  S([start]) --> MC[manage_context]
  MC --> AG[agent]
  AG -- "no tool calls" --> E([end])
  AG -- "safe tools" --> TL[tools]
  AG -- "risky tools" --> HA{{"human_approval
interrupt()"}}
  HA -- "approve / edit" --> TL
  HA -- "reject + feedback" --> AG
  TL --> AG
  • manage_context — summarizes if the history is too long.
  • agent — calls the model with bound tools.
  • tools — ToolNode runs all safe tool calls in parallel.
  • human_approval — pauses with interrupt() for risky tools.

docs.title: The Documents (agentic RAG) graph
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  S([start]) --> MC[manage_context] --> P[prepare] --> R[retrieve] --> GR[grade]
  GR -- "sufficient" --> GE[generate]
  GR -- "insufficient, rewrites < 2" --> RW[rewrite] --> R
  GE --> E([end])
  • grade — asks the model if the retrieved docs answer the question.
  • rewrite — if not, rewrites the query and retrieves again (max 2 rewrites).
  • generate — answers with inline citations.

docs.title: The Researcher graph
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  S([start]) --> MC[manage_context] --> PL[planner]
  PL --> AP{{"approve_plan
interrupt()"}}
  AP -- cancel --> CA[cancel] --> E([end])
  AP -- approve/edit --> FAN["Send() × N steps"]
  FAN --> W1[research_one]
  FAN --> W2[research_one]
  W1 --> WR[writer]
  W2 --> WR
  WR --> E

Send is LangGraph's way to fan out: it creates one instance of research_one per plan step, all running in parallel, with their own input payload. The findings reducer (a custom Annotated field) appends results from all workers.

docs.title: Run configuration
docs.text:
Every graph is compiled once at startup. Per-request options (model, tools, approval toggle) are passed through config["configurable"] and read by AgentConfig:

cfg = AgentConfig.from_config(config)
llm = get_chat_model(cfg.provider, cfg.model, cfg.temperature)

This means one compiled graph serves every provider and model combination — no restart needed to switch.

docs.title: Scaling out
docs.text:
SQLite is single-process. For multiple replicas:

# services/checkpointer.py
from langgraph.checkpoint.postgres.aio import AsyncPostgresSaver
async with AsyncPostgresSaver.from_conn_string(database_url) as saver:
    await saver.setup()
    yield saver

Install langgraph-checkpoint-postgres and psycopg[binary,pool].

docs.title: LCEL Chains
docs.text:
LCEL (LangChain Expression Language) lets you compose processing steps with the | operator. Every step is a Runnable — they share one interface, so they compose freely.

Source file: backend/app/chains/lcel.py

docs.title: 1. Prompt | model | parser
docs.text:
The simplest pattern: a prompt template, a chat model, and a string parser piped together.

from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", "Summarize the text in {style}."),
    ("human", "{text}"),
])

chain = prompt | llm | StrOutputParser()
result = await chain.ainvoke({"text": "...", "style": "3 bullet points"})

The | operator calls .pipe() under the hood and returns a new Runnable. You can call .invoke(), .ainvoke(), .stream(), .astream() or .batch() on the result.

docs.title: 2. Structured output
docs.text:
Instead of parsing free text, ask the model to return a Pydantic object:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Entities(BaseModel):
    people: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
    organizations: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
    locations: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)

chain = prompt | llm.with_structured_output(Entities)
result = await chain.ainvoke({"text": "Apple was founded by Steve Jobs in Cupertino."})
# result.people == ["Steve Jobs"]
# result.organizations == ["Apple"]
# result.locations == ["Cupertino"]

.with_structured_output() uses function calling under the hood when the provider supports it, or falls back to JSON mode. It returns a validated Pydantic instance — no parsing code needed.

docs.title: 3. RunnableParallel — fan out, collect
docs.text:
Run multiple chains on the same input simultaneously:

from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableParallel

chain = RunnableParallel(
    summary=summary_chain,
    keywords=keyword_chain,
    sentiment=sentiment_chain,
)
result = await chain.ainvoke({"text": "..."})
# result == {"summary": "...", "keywords": "...", "sentiment": {...}}

All three branches run concurrently. The output is a dict keyed by name.

docs.title: 4. RunnableBranch — routing
docs.text:
Route to different chains based on the input:

from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableBranch

branch = RunnableBranch(
    (lambda x: "code" in x["topic"],   code_specialist_chain),
    (lambda x: "math" in x["topic"],   math_specialist_chain),
    general_chain,          # default
)

This project uses a classifier LLM call first, then branches on the classified topic:

router = (
    {"topic": classifier_chain, "question": lambda x: x["question"]}
    | branch
)

docs.title: 5. RunnableLambda — arbitrary Python
docs.text:
Wrap any function as a Runnable step:

from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda

format_docs = RunnableLambda(lambda docs: "\n\n".join(d.page_content for d in docs))

docs.title: 6. Retries and fallbacks
docs.text:
# Retry up to 3 times on transient errors (rate limits, timeouts)
robust = llm.with_retry(stop_after_attempt=3, wait_exponential_jitter=True)

# Fall back to a second model if the first keeps failing
resilient = robust.with_fallbacks([backup_llm])

docs.title: Try it in the UI
docs.text: Go to the Chains tab in the sidebar. Pick a chain, fill in the fields, and click Run chain. The output appears below. Read the source in backend/app/chains/lcel.py alongside this page — every chain is ~10 lines.

docs.title: Memory — Short & Long Term
docs.text: The project uses two separate memory systems that work together.

docs.title: Short-term memory — conversation history
docs.text:
Short-term memory is the message history in AgentState.messages. It is persisted in the SQLite checkpointer, keyed by thread_id.

Thread A  ──► checkpoint A: [HumanMessage, AIMessage, HumanMessage, ...]
Thread B  ──► checkpoint B: [HumanMessage, AIMessage, ...]

Every time you send a message, the graph loads the checkpoint for that thread, appends the new message, runs, and saves the updated state back.

When the history gets too long, manage_context summarizes it — see Context Management.

Scope: one conversation thread. Survives restart: yes (SQLite).

docs.title: Long-term memory — the store
docs.text:
Long-term memory is a key-value store shared across all threads for a user. The agent can read and write it with two tools:

Tool When to use it save_memory "Remember that I prefer dark mode." search_memory Recalled automatically when personalizing answers.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
@tool
async def save_memory(
    content: str,
    config: RunnableConfig,
    store: Annotated[BaseStore, InjectedStore()],
) -> str:
    """Save a durable fact or preference about the user."""
    user_id = config["configurable"].get("user_id", "default")
    await store.aput(("memories", user_id), str(uuid.uuid4()), {"content": content})
    return f"Saved: {content}"

Memories are namespaced under ("memories", user_id) so different users cannot see each other's memories.

docs.title: Viewing and deleting memories
docs.text: Open Settings → Long-term memory in the UI. You can see every saved fact and delete individual ones. The /api/memory endpoint also exposes them directly.

docs.title: Default store — in-memory
docs.text:
By default the project uses InMemoryStore, which is fast but does not persist across server restarts.

# backend/app/main.py
store = InMemoryStore()

docs.title: Upgrading to persistent storage
docs.text:
For production, replace with a Postgres-backed store:

# install: pip install langgraph-checkpoint-postgres psycopg[binary,pool]
from langgraph.store.postgres.aio import AsyncPostgresStore

store = AsyncPostgresStore.from_conn_string(settings.database_url)
await store.setup()   # creates tables

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Short-term Long-term What Conversation messages Facts and preferences Where LangGraph checkpointer LangGraph store Keyed by thread_id (user_id, memory_id) Scope One thread All threads for a user Persists Yes (SQLite) No by default — use Postgres How accessed Automatic save_memory / search_memory tools

docs.title: Concepts Overview
docs.text: This project is a complete, working implementation of the major LangChain and LangGraph patterns. This section explains each concept with diagrams, code excerpts and links to the relevant source files.

docs.title: The LangChain stack
docs.text:
Your application
       │
       ▼
langchain-core          ← abstractions: chat models, tools, prompts, output parsers
       │
       ├── langchain            ← chains, agents, memory utilities
       ├── langchain-community  ← loaders, vector stores, third-party integrations
       ├── langchain-openai     ← OpenAI models and embeddings
       ├── langchain-anthropic  ← Anthropic Claude
       ├── langchain-google-genai  ← Google Gemini
       └── ...                  ← one package per provider
       │
langgraph               ← stateful, multi-step, branching agent graphs

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text: If you want to understand… Read How LCEL chains work LCEL Chains How LangGraph agents work LangGraph Agents How human approval works Human-in-the-Loop How documents are indexed and searched RAG How long conversations are handled Context Management What tools are available Tools How to add a new provider Providers How memory works Memory How tokens stream to the browser Streaming How token usage is tracked Callbacks

docs.title: LLM Providers
docs.text:
The project supports 8 providers through a single factory function. Switching provider is a UI dropdown — no code change or restart needed.

Source files: backend/app/llm/factory.py, backend/app/llm/catalog.py

docs.title: Supported providers
docs.text:
OpenAIAnthropicGoogle GeminiDeepSeekxAI GrokOpenRouterGroqOllama (local) 

OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
DEFAULT_PROVIDER=openai
DEFAULT_MODEL=gpt-4o-mini
Suggested models: gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4o, gpt-4.1, o4-mini

ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
DEFAULT_PROVIDER=anthropic
DEFAULT_MODEL=claude-sonnet-5-5
Suggested models: claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-opus-5-5, claude-haiku-5-5

GOOGLE_API_KEY=AIza...
DEFAULT_PROVIDER=gemini
DEFAULT_MODEL=gemini-2.5-flash
Suggested models: gemini-2.5-flash, gemini-2.5-pro, gemini-2.0-flash

DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=...
DEFAULT_PROVIDER=deepseek
DEFAULT_MODEL=deepseek-chat
Suggested models: deepseek-chat, deepseek-reasoner

deepseek-reasoner

deepseek-reasoner streams its internal reasoning into a collapsible block in the UI. Check your provider's current docs for tool-calling support.

XAI_API_KEY=xai-...
DEFAULT_PROVIDER=xai
DEFAULT_MODEL=grok-3
Suggested models: grok-4, grok-3, grok-3-mini

OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...
DEFAULT_PROVIDER=openrouter
DEFAULT_MODEL=openai/gpt-4o-mini
OpenRouter is an OpenAI-compatible gateway to 200+ models. Model ids are vendor/model, e.g. anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.5, meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct.

GROQ_API_KEY=gsk_...
DEFAULT_PROVIDER=groq
DEFAULT_MODEL=llama-3.3-70b-versatile
Groq serves open-source models with extremely low latency.

OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434
DEFAULT_PROVIDER=ollama
DEFAULT_MODEL=llama3.2
No API key. Run ollama pull llama3.2 (or any model) first.

docs.title: How the factory works
docs.text:
def get_chat_model(provider: str, model: str, temperature: float = 0.2) -> BaseChatModel:
    key = resolve_api_key(provider)   # per-request key first, then .env
    if provider == "openai":
        from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
        return ChatOpenAI(model=model, temperature=temperature, api_key=key)
    if provider == "openrouter":
        from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
        return ChatOpenAI(model=model, api_key=key, base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1")
    # ... one branch per provider

All providers are imported lazily. Missing a package only breaks that provider, not the whole app.

docs.title: Adding a provider
docs.text:
1. Add a ProviderSpec in backend/app/llm/catalog.py:

    "myprovider": ProviderSpec(
    "myprovider", "My Provider",
    ["model-a", "model-b"],
    docs_url="https://myprovider.com/docs",
),

  2. Add a branch in backend/app/llm/factory.py:

    if provider == "myprovider":
    from langchain_myprovider import ChatMyProvider
    return ChatMyProvider(model=model, temperature=temperature, api_key=key)

  3. Add myprovider_api_key to Settings and provider_keys in backend/app/core/config.py.

For OpenAI-compatible APIs (like OpenRouter), step 2 is just ChatOpenAI(base_url=..., api_key=...).

docs.title: Per-request keys
docs.text: Keys pasted in the UI travel in the request body and are stored in a ContextVar — they are never written to the database or checkpointer. resolve_api_key prefers the per-request key and falls back to the server environment key.

docs.title: RAG — Document Intelligence
docs.text:
RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) lets the model answer questions using your own documents rather than its training data. This project implements an agentic RAG pipeline — one that checks its own work and rewrites the query if the first retrieval fails.

Source files: backend/app/rag/, backend/app/agents/rag_agent.py

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
Upload → Load → Split → Embed → Store (Chroma)
                                      │
Query  ──────────────────────────► Retrieve (MMR)
                                      │
                                   Grade (LLM)
                                      │
                             sufficient? ──no──► Rewrite query ──► Retrieve again
                                      │
                                    yes
                                      │
                                  Generate (LLM) + cite sources

docs.title: Supported file types
docs.text: Extension Loader .pdf PyPDFLoader (one Document per page) .txt, .md, .markdown Plain text .csv, .json Plain text

docs.title: Chunking
docs.text:
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=1000,    # configured via CHUNK_SIZE
    chunk_overlap=150,  # configured via CHUNK_OVERLAP
)
chunks = splitter.split_documents(docs)

RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter tries to split on paragraph breaks, then sentences, then words — so chunks are semantically coherent.

docs.title: Re-uploading
docs.text:
Re-uploading a file with the same name deletes the old chunks first:

store._collection.delete(where={"source": display_name})
store.add_documents(chunks)

docs.title: Embeddings
docs.text:
Controlled by EMBEDDINGS_PROVIDER in .env:

Provider Default model Package openai text-embedding-3-small langchain-openai google models/gemini-embedding-001 langchain-google-genai ollama nomic-embed-text langchain-ollama huggingface all-MiniLM-L6-v2 langchain-huggingface

docs.title: Vector store — Chroma
docs.text:
from langchain_chroma import Chroma

vectorstore = Chroma(
    collection_name="knowledge_base",
    embedding_function=get_embeddings(),
    persist_directory="./data/chroma",   # persists to disk
)

Chroma stores vectors locally in data/chroma/. No external service needed.

docs.title: Retrieval — MMR
docs.text:
MMR (Maximal Marginal Relevance) balances relevance and diversity — it avoids returning five near-identical chunks:

retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever(
    search_type="mmr",
    search_kwargs={"k": 4, "fetch_k": 16},  # fetch 16, keep 4 most diverse
)

docs.title: Agentic loop
docs.text:
The Documents agent adds two extra steps around retrieval:

Grade — the model judges whether the retrieved chunks actually answer the question:

class Grade(BaseModel):
    sufficient: bool
    reason: str

verdict = await llm.with_structured_output(Grade).ainvoke(
    f"Question: {question}\n\nDocuments: {context}\n\nDo these answer the question?"
)

Rewrite — if not sufficient (max 2 rewrites):

better_query = await llm.ainvoke(
    f"Rewrite this as a better search query: {question}"
)

docs.title: Citations
docs.text:
Every retrieved chunk carries metadata. generate returns sources:

[
  {"index": 1, "source": "report.pdf", "page": 3, "snippet": "...first 240 chars..."},
  {"index": 2, "source": "notes.md",   "page": null, "snippet": "..."},
]

The model is instructed to cite sources as [1], [2] inline. The UI renders them as expandable source cards below the answer.

docs.title: One-shot vs. agentic
docs.text: One-shot (POST /api/rag/query) Agentic (Documents agent in Chat) Loop Single retrieval Retrieve → grade → (rewrite) → retrieve Multi-turn No Yes — tracks conversation history Use for Quick lookups Deep Q&A over documents

docs.title: Streaming & SSE
docs.text:
The project streams agent output token-by-token over Server-Sent Events (SSE). SSE is a lightweight HTTP streaming protocol — the server sends a never-ending response with data: frames, and the browser reads them live.

Source file: backend/app/services/streaming.py

docs.title: Why SSE, not WebSockets?
docs.text: SSE is one-directional (server → client) and works over plain HTTP/1.1 — no upgrade handshake, no socket management, no CORS complications. For a chat app where the server pushes tokens and the client posts messages, SSE is simpler and more reliable.

docs.title: The event stream
docs.text:
Every run produces a stream of small JSON objects. The browser reconstructs the UI from these events:

data: {"type": "start", "thread_id": "abc123"}

data: {"type": "step", "node": "manage_context"}

data: {"type": "tool_call", "id": "call_1", "name": "web_search", "args": {"query": "..."}}

data: {"type": "token", "content": "According", "node": "agent"}
data: {"type": "token", "content": " to", "node": "agent"}
data: {"type": "token", "content": " Wikipedia", "node": "agent"}

data: {"type": "tool_result", "tool_call_id": "call_1", "name": "web_search", "content": "...", "status": "success"}

data: {"type": "usage", "input_tokens": 412, "output_tokens": 89, "total_tokens": 501, "llm_calls": 2}

data: {"type": "done", "interrupted": false}

See the full event reference in Stream Events.

docs.title: How the backend streams
docs.text:
LangGraph's astream() supports multiple stream modes simultaneously:

async for mode, data in graph.astream(
    graph_input, config,
    stream_mode=["messages", "updates"],
):
    if mode == "messages":
        chunk, meta = data
        # AIMessageChunk — stream tokens only from designated nodes
        if meta["langgraph_node"] in stream_nodes and isinstance(chunk, AIMessageChunk):
            yield {"type": "token", "content": chunk.content}

    elif mode == "updates":
        for node, update in data.items():
            yield {"type": "step", "node": node}
            yield from events_from_update(node, update)

stream_mode="messages" delivers token-level deltas. stream_mode="updates" delivers completed node outputs (tool calls, tool results, plans, sources).

docs.title: Controlling which nodes stream
docs.text:
Only nodes in AGENTS[agent]["stream_nodes"] produce token events:

AGENTS = {
    "assistant":  {"stream_nodes": {"agent"}},
    "rag":        {"stream_nodes": {"generate"}},
    "research":   {"stream_nodes": {"writer", "cancel"}},
}

Internal LLM calls (grading relevance, planning, summarizing) don't leak into the chat.

docs.title: How the frontend reads the stream
docs.text:
fetch() is used instead of EventSource because EventSource only supports GET, and sending a message body requires POST:

const res = await fetch("/api/chat/stream", {
    method: "POST",
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
});
const reader = res.body.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream()).getReader();
let buffer = "";
for (;;) {
    const { value, done } = await reader.read();
    if (done) break;
    buffer += value;
    while (buffer.includes("\n\n")) {
        const [frame, ...rest] = buffer.split("\n\n");
        buffer = rest.join("\n\n");
        const data = frame.split("\n").filter(l => l.startsWith("data: ")).map(l => l.slice(6)).join("");
        onEvent(JSON.parse(data));
    }
}

docs.title: Proxy buffering — the most common problem
docs.text:
If streaming appears all at once instead of incrementally, a proxy is buffering the response. Add to your nginx config:

location /api/ {
    proxy_buffering off;
    proxy_cache off;
    proxy_read_timeout 600s;
}

The project's frontend/nginx.conf already includes this.

docs.title: Tools & Registry
docs.text:
Tools are functions the model can call to take actions in the world. The project ships 14 tools across 6 categories, all registered in one file.

Source files: backend/app/tools/

docs.title: Tool catalog
docs.text: Tool Category Needs approval Description web_search web DuckDuckGo — no key needed wikipedia web Introduction of the best-matching article fetch_url web Readable text of a public page get_weather web Open-Meteo — no key needed calculator utility AST-based, no eval() get_current_datetime utility Any IANA timezone search_knowledge_base knowledge Searches your uploaded documents save_memory memory Saves a fact to long-term memory search_memory memory Recalls facts from long-term memory list_files files Lists the agent workspace read_file files Reads a file from the workspace write_file files ✅ Writes to the workspace python_repl code ✅ Runs Python in a subprocess with a timeout send_email communication ✅ Simulated: writes to data/workspace/outbox.jsonl

docs.title: Defining a tool
docs.text:
Every tool is a @tool-decorated function. The docstring is what the model reads to decide when to use it.

from langchain_core.tools import tool

@tool
def calculator(expression: str) -> str:
    """Evaluate a math expression exactly. Supports +, -, *, /, **, sqrt, sin, cos,
    log, factorial, abs, round, min, max, pi, e.
    Example: "sqrt(144) + 2**10"."""
    try:
        return str(safe_eval(expression))
    except Exception as exc:
        return f"Could not evaluate '{expression}': {exc}"

Write a clear, specific docstring — it is the model's only documentation for the tool.

docs.title: The tool registry
docs.text:
backend/app/tools/registry.py centralises all tool metadata:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ToolSpec:
    tool: BaseTool
    category: str
    requires_approval: bool = False

_SPECS = [
    ToolSpec(calculator,  "utility"),
    ToolSpec(python_repl, "code",          requires_approval=True),
    ToolSpec(send_email,  "communication", requires_approval=True),
    # ...
]

The registry drives the Settings panel in the UI (tool checkboxes), the /api/tools endpoint, and the approval routing logic. To toggle a tool's approval requirement, change requires_approval here.

docs.title: Adding a tool
docs.text:
Step 1. Write the tool in backend/app/tools/your_tool.py:

from langchain_core.tools import tool

@tool
def my_tool(param: str) -> str:
    """One sentence explaining when to call this tool."""
    return do_something(param)

Step 2. Register it in backend/app/tools/registry.py:

from app.tools.your_tool import my_tool

_SPECS = [
    ...
    ToolSpec(my_tool, "utility"),                         # auto-approved
    ToolSpec(my_tool, "utility", requires_approval=True), # pauses for human
]

Step 3. Add a friendly label in frontend/src/lib/labels.ts (optional):

const TOOL_LABELS: Record<string, [string, string]> = {
    my_tool: ["Running my tool", "Ran my tool"],
};

That is all — the tool appears in the Settings panel and the trace rail automatically.

docs.title: Tools with injected state
docs.text:
Some tools need access to the LangGraph store (for long-term memory) or the run config. Use InjectedStore and RunnableConfig:

from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableConfig
from langchain_core.tools import tool
from langgraph.prebuilt import InjectedStore
from langgraph.store.base import BaseStore
from typing import Annotated

@tool
async def save_memory(
    content: str,
    config: RunnableConfig,
    store: Annotated[BaseStore, InjectedStore()],
) -> str:
    """Save a durable fact about the user."""
    user_id = config["configurable"].get("user_id", "default")
    await store.aput(("memories", user_id), str(uuid.uuid4()), {"content": content})
    return f"Saved: {content}"

LangGraph injects config and store automatically — the model only sees and fills content.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• calculator — uses a safe AST evaluator, not eval(). It cannot import modules or access the filesystem.
  • fetch_url — resolves the hostname and refuses private/loopback addresses (SSRF protection).
  • python_repl — runs in a subprocess with a configurable timeout. This is not a real sandbox. For production, use a container, gVisor or a hosted sandbox like E2B.
  • write_file, read_file, list_files — confined to data/workspace via path resolution. A path like ../../etc/passwd raises a ValueError.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
All settings are environment variables, read from .env in the repo root.

cp .env.example .env

docs.title: Provider keys
docs.text:
Variable Provider Docs OPENAI_API_KEY OpenAI platform.openai.com ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Anthropic console.anthropic.com GOOGLE_API_KEY Google Gemini aistudio.google.com DEEPSEEK_API_KEY DeepSeek platform.deepseek.com XAI_API_KEY xAI Grok console.x.ai OPENROUTER_API_KEY OpenRouter openrouter.ai/keys GROQ_API_KEY Groq console.groq.com OLLAMA_BASE_URL Ollama No key — default http://localhost:11434

All keys are optional at the server level. Users can also paste a key in the Settings panel — it is stored in the browser only and sent per-request, never persisted on the server.

docs.text:
DEFAULT_PROVIDER=openai
DEFAULT_MODEL=gpt-4o-mini

No OpenAI key?

Set EMBEDDINGS_PROVIDER=ollama or huggingface so document upload works without an OpenAI key.

docs.title: Docker Deployment
docs.text:
cp .env.example .env    # add your provider keys
docker compose up --build
# open http://localhost:8080

The first build takes 2–4 minutes. Subsequent starts are fast.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Container Image Port backend python:3.12-slim internal :8000 frontend nginx:1.27-alpine host :8080

Nginx serves the compiled React app and proxies /api to the backend with buffering disabled.

docs.title: Data persistence
docs.text:
Conversations, the vector store and the agent workspace live in the app-data Docker volume.

docker compose down      # stop, keep data
docker compose down -v   # stop and delete data

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Set API_AUTH_TOKEN in .env
  • Set ENVIRONMENT=production
  • Use HTTPS with a reverse proxy (Caddy / nginx)
  • Disable buffering and set a long read timeout on /api paths
  • Back up the app-data volume

docs.title: Your First Conversation
docs.text: A guided walkthrough of each feature.

docs.title: Safe tool use
docs.text:
Try: "What is sqrt(1764) plus 10% of 500?"

  • The agent uses the calculator tool.
  • A trace rail appears beside the reply showing the tool call and result.
  • Expand any node to inspect the exact arguments and output.

docs.title: Human-in-the-loop approval
docs.text:
Try: "Email ceo@example.com a one-line meeting reminder."

  1. A saffron approval gate appears — the run is paused.
  2. You see the tool name and its arguments in an editable JSON box.
  3. Approve to run as-is, edit the JSON then approve to change arguments, or reject with feedback.
  4. After approving, the trace rail updates and the reply completes.

Tip

Disable approvals for a session with the Human in the loop toggle in Settings.

docs.title: Documents agent
docs.text:
1. Go to Documents in the sidebar and upload a PDF or text file.
  2. Switch the agent to Documents in Chat.
  3. Ask a question — the agent retrieves chunks, checks relevance, and answers with [1] [2] citations you can expand.

docs.title: Researcher agent
docs.text:
Try: "Research open-source LLMs in 2025."

  1. A plan appears — 2–4 research steps.
  2. An approval gate lets you edit steps or cancel.
  3. Steps execute in parallel.
  4. The writer produces a structured Markdown report with sources.

docs.title: Settings panel
docs.text:
• Provider / Model — switch at any time; type any model id your provider supports.
  • API key — paste a per-session key stored only in your browser.
  • Instructions — a custom system prompt for this session.
  • Tools — enable or disable individual tools.
  • Long-term memory — view and delete saved facts.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Get the project running locally in under five minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.11+
  • Node.js 20+
  • Git
  • An API key for at least one provider, or Ollama running locally

docs.title: 1. Clone and install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/javaidgithub/langchain-ai-project.git
cd langchain-ai-project
make setup

make setup copies .env.example → .env, creates a Python venv, installs all Python packages, and runs npm install.

No make?

cp .env.example .env
cd backend && python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && pip install -r requirements.txt
cd ../frontend && npm install

docs.title: 2. Add a provider key
docs.text:
Open .env and add at least one key:

OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
# or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
# or DEFAULT_PROVIDER=ollama  (no key needed with Ollama)

No API key? Use Ollama

Install Ollama, run ollama pull llama3.2, then set: 

DEFAULT_PROVIDER=ollama
DEFAULT_MODEL=llama3.2
EMBEDDINGS_PROVIDER=ollama

docs.title: 3. Start the servers
docs.text:
make backend    # terminal 1 — API on http://localhost:8000
make frontend   # terminal 2 — UI  on http://localhost:5173

Open http://localhost:5173.

docs.title: 4. Quick Docker alternative
docs.text:
cp .env.example .env   # add your keys
docker compose up --build
# open http://localhost:8080
